::: {.solutions}

**Show all your reasoning.** Total: **32 marks** · Suggested time: **45 minutes**.

This tests the cards on the [T2 concepts page](t02_shapes_as_logic.qmd) — the quadrilateral lattice, the
diagonal table, the congruence criteria and the three standard counterexamples. Close that page first.

::: {.callout-important}
## What earns the marks

**Do not try to prove these.** Reach for a **named shape**.

Every "not sufficient" verdict wants a specific figure — *a rhombus that is not a square*, *a rectangle that
is not a square*, *an isosceles trapezium* — and saying which of its properties fails. A verdict with no
named shape scores the method mark at most.

Every "necessary and sufficient" claim needs **both directions** argued separately.
:::

| Section | What it covers | Marks |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Recall** | the lattice, the diagonal table, the counterexamples | 8 |
| **B — Standard** | conditions on quadrilaterals and triangles | 16 |
| **C — Stretch** | two results you derive yourself | 8 |

## Question 2 **[4]**

::: {.question}
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral. For each diagonal condition, name the shape it guarantees — and say whether the
condition is **necessary**, **sufficient**, or **both**, for that shape.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) The diagonals bisect each other. **[1]**
&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) The diagonals bisect each other and are equal in length. **[1]**
&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) The diagonals bisect each other and are perpendicular. **[1]**
&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) The diagonals are perpendicular. **[1]**
:::

## Question 6 **[4]**

::: {.question}
&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Write down the sum of the interior angles of an $n$-sided polygon, and the interior angle
of a **regular** $n$-gon. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) The five interior angles of a pentagon form an arithmetic sequence. Prove that one of them
must be exactly $108^\circ$, whatever the common difference. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Hence decide whether this statement is true, and whether its **converse** is true: *"if at

## Question 8 **[4]**

::: {.question}
A polygon with $n\ge3$ vertices is inscribed in a circle whose centre lies **inside** it. The $n$ radii to
the vertices cut the polygon into $n$ triangles, and **all $n$ triangles have equal area**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Writing $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n$ for the central angles, show that the equal-area condition
forces each $\theta_i$ to be **$\alpha$ or $180^\circ-\alpha$** for some fixed $\alpha$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Hence show that the polygon must be regular when $n=3$, but need not be when $n=4$. **[2]**
:::

## Before you hand this in

1. Every **"not sufficient"** should have a **named shape** beside it, and the property it fails.
2. Every **"necessary and sufficient"** should have **two** arguments, one per direction.
3. Wherever you recovered an angle from a sine, check you considered **both** $\theta$ and
   $180^\circ-\theta$.
